content_voiceover: Now antithrombin, labeled A T, is overlaid onto the same cascade diagram, and you can see it acts at multiple points simultaneously. Antithrombin directly inhibits factor Xa within both the extrinsic and intrinsic tenase-generated pools, inhibits thrombin, FIIa, itself, and also inhibits factor XIa. This broad specificity is what makes antithrombin the master regulator of coagulation: rather than blocking one enzyme, it neutralizes the serine proteases at nearly every step of the cascade. Clinically, this is the same antithrombin that heparin potentiates; heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates its inhibitory activity by roughly a thousand fold, which is the pharmacologic basis for using unfractionated and low molecular weight heparin as anticoagulants. Inherited antithrombin deficiency is also a classic tested cause of venous thromboembolism, and it explains why some patients appear heparin resistant.
keypoints: Antithrombin inhibits factor Xa, thrombin (FIIa), and factor XIa
Broad specificity across multiple cascade steps
Heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates inhibition about 1000-fold
Antithrombin deficiency is a classic inherited thrombophilia and cause of heparin resistance
keypoint_voiceover: Antithrombin is a broad-spectrum serine protease inhibitor hitting factor Xa, thrombin, and factor XIa. Heparin dramatically accelerates its activity, which is the mechanistic basis of heparin therapy. Inherited antithrombin deficiency causes thrombophilia and can produce apparent heparin resistance, a classic boards pairing.
